title: There Is No ‘Nordic Model’
author: Felice Basbøll
content:
![There Is No ‘Nordic
Model’](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/The_Little_Mermaid_in_Copenhagen-_2013.jpg)

Nordic cultural capital is at an all-time high. But the "Nordic" export is
more of a vibe than a specific flavor profile or iconography. Most trendy
shopping districts will have a Nordic concept cafe or a fashion house;
department stores will carry a "Scandi" line, often with little relationship
to anything Scandinavians would tend to have in their homes. The concept of
_hygge_ as a way of life is Denmark's most recognizable export. But its
meaning--rougly "making ordinary, everyday things more meaningful, beautiful,
or special"--is equivalent to "in my culture, we value food and family."

Nordic coffee bars are less likely to be run by Scandinavians than by people
who believe their home countries could benefit from some Nordic "slow living."
Drip coffee has become a symbol of appreciation for noticing your surroundings
and everyday processes, all the things the screens have taken away.
Scandinavians like errands, value their time off, and take pride in filling it
with the mundane. Their mix of modern interior design and progressive politics
usefully permits things like home making, country living, knitting, and
sourdough to be decoupled from the trad wife aesthetic.

The appeal of Nordic aesthetics was always bound up with the political ideal
represented by the region's generous welfare systems and egalitarian ethic.
Men push baby carriages and the state provides generous maternity and
paternity leave. Always leading in foreign aid contributions, Nordics consider
themselves humanitarian frontrunners. On climate, too, Denmark is a key
exporter of windmills, and Sweden gave the world Greta Thunberg. The education
system has little stratification, and most institutions aim at making young
Scandinavians "good enough." No one should get too big for our shared boots.
We are far more comfortable being dependent on the state than on each other.
The Nordics have grown in appeal as "well-being" has replaced liberty as a
primary target for measuring human flourishing.

However, it is becoming harder and harder to see the Nordic countries as
representative of a single "model." Denmark's big companies like Novo Nordisk
and Maersk are a source of national pride, but new start-ups quickly move
their operations elsewhere. Sweden and Iceland, by contrast, have the highest
numbers of tech "unicorns" outside the United States and Israel. On
immigration policy, meanwhile, the Nordics are far from a unified bloc. Sweden
welcomed Syrian refugees while Denmark pulled up the draw bridges. Only now
are the other Nordic countries following suit.

People do not open up a Nordic-style cafe because they admire Mette
Frederiksen's record on immigration policy, but in recent years, Denmark has
gained some cachet on the right. This is no small feat; as much as the Nordic
model was admired and invoked by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez,
the "socialist" states of Northern Europe have been longstanding bogeymen for
the American right. Many decades back, President Eisenhower took a swipe at
Sweden for being overrun with paternalism and drunkenness: "Lack of ambition
is discernible on all sides," he said. But today, the Nordics have started to
look more promising to a new postliberal right that hymns community, trust,
and strong culture.

> "We're happy to forgo such comforts."

There are natural barriers to immigration in Denmark that are hard to
reproduce in the Anglosphere. Danes speak English, today's lingua franca, but
speaking Danish is necessary in order to settle and thrive long-term. The
egalitarian ethic is enticing at a distance, when it is constrained to your
local cafe, but somewhat less so when it comes with the heavy tax burden and
few paths to excellence. As a result, there are high levels of short-term
high-skilled immigration; people leave when they can no longer stand it. We
have fewer Deliveroo drivers and cleaners, because we like housekeeping and
running errands, and because these services are more expensive on Scandinavian
wages. We're happy to forgo such comforts.

Denmark's hard line on immigration is a question of pragmatism more than
principle. A favorite refrain in Danish politics is that a policy must not
lead to "absurd" outcomes. Policies are directed at fixing specific problems;
[_anti-ghetto laws_](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/dec/18/denmark-
ghetto-law-parallel-societies-may-be-unlawful-eu?ref=compactmag.com), which
allow the government to carry out evictions and demolitions in areas that are
more than 50 percent "non-Western," are no exception. These policies were
designed expressly to avoid "Swedish conditions"--the pockets of violence that
our neighbor nation has allowed to fester.

For similar reasons, the Nordic economic model has come a long way since its
socialist beginnings. Scandinavian countries have a generous benefit system,
but very few worker protections. The Danes pay far more in taxes, but
Britain's tax system is far more progressive. Even the children of the
wealthiest Danes receive a generous government grant as students. A third of
apartments in Copenhagen are so-called _andelsboliger_ , which are part-owned
through an association. These used to provide housing for the working class,
but in practice, because they are passed on by knowing someone who knows
someone, they have become
[_hotbeds_](https://politiken.dk/danmark/oekonomi/privatoekonomi/art10400186/S%C3%A6lger-
blev-d%C3%B8mt-til-at-betale-overprisen-tilbage?ref=compactmag.com) of
nepotism and corruption. Just before the 2026 election, the government
announced a _f ødevarechek_, or food allowance, in order to combat rising cost
of living prices, which was paid out to a third of the Danish population.
Political opponents criticized the payout as tantamount to bribery.

Beneath the surface, Scandinavia is very far from the dreams of the left and
the right. The Nordic tradeoff in the twentieth century was to retain old-
fashioned institutions, but without their spiritual heft. Generous welfare
provisions ensure that Scandinavians are never interpersonally financially
dependent on each other, and even married couples file their taxes as
individuals. The _f ødevarechek_ was given to some Danish millionaire
households for this reason: Distribution was based on individual rather than
household income. We may on paper be more religious--70 percent of Danes are
members of the Danish national church**--** and collectivist, but in practice
we have religion without God and marriage without dependency. We have little
responsibility for each other beyond our tax payments.

In a 1955 article in _Time_ , a Swedish man was quoted as saying: "The only
difference between our behavior here and behavior in other countries is that
we face the facts." He was referring to acceptance of sex before marriage, but
Scandinavians pride themselves on their pragmatism on a wide range of issues.
Denmark is a country run on egalitarianism, soft nepotism, and
"reasonableness," and it wouldn't work otherwise. Sweden embraces its own
contradictions by preserving socialist vibes in an increasingly libertarian
business environment. Finland famously earns its title as the happiest country
in the world by having [_low expectations_](https://slate.com/news-and-
politics/2021/04/finland-happiness-lagom-hygge.html?ref=compactmag.com).
Perhaps there is something to admire in this flexibility, but it is no
"model."
